messages:
kai: Anyone else seeing pods that explicitly tolerate gpu taints end up on CPU nodes after the scheduler bump this morning? Started ~06:12 UTC.

marta: yup, noticed a burst in us-west. Pods were Pending for ~20s then landed on non-gpu nodes. Weird part: they had the toleration in the pod spec.

kai: here's an example pod yaml (sanitized):
```
spec:
  tolerations:
  - key: "node.kubernetes.io/gpu"
    operator: "Exists"
    effect: "NoSchedule"
  nodeSelector:
    workload: "inference"
```
Nodes show taint `accelerator=present:NoSchedule` and label `accelerator.type=nvidia-a100`.

marta: our older node provisioning used taint key `node.kubernetes.io/gpu` but the new nodegroup bootstrap uses `accelerator=present` to be cloud-agnostic. Pod tolerations still target the old key, so scheduler treats them as tolerating nothing. But why did pods still schedule to CPU nodes rather than stay pending?

ryan: scheduler has a fallback path when nodeAffinity/selector can't be satisfied: if there are nodes that match selectors but taints are tolerated, it will pick those. If tolerations don't match, normally it shouldn't schedule. Are you seeing any mutated pod spec or admission changes?

infra-bot: [autoscaler] scaleUp request 3->5 for ng-gpu-usw2 at 06:13 UTC (reason: pods unschedulable due to Insufficient accelerators). Attempted provisioning of nodes with label accelerator.type=nvidia-a100.

sasha: dug in logs — kube-scheduler logs show it evaluated node predicates in a different order after the patch. There's also a mutating webhook that rewrites nodeSelector to `workload: inference:legacy` for some older deployments. That rewrite bypassed the more specific nodeAffinity block, leaving selector matching CPU nodes that had the legacy label.

marta: aha. so three interacting things: 1) taint key rename on nodes, 2) mutating webhook rewriting nodeSelector to a legacy label, 3) scheduler predicate ordering change. Combined allowed pods to be considered "matching" CPU nodes even though they didn't actually have GPUs.

kai: quick mitigation: two options — (A) add a toleration for `accelerator` taint key in the pod templates (fast), or (B) patch the nodegroup bootstrap to add the old taint key alongside the new one (safer long-term). I'll run (A) as a canary on the failing deployment.

marta: can you share the kubectl patch you used? I'll apply to a dev deployment first.

kai: sure:
```
kubectl -n model deploy patch inference-deploy -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"tolerations":[{"key":"accelerator","operator":"Exists","effect":"NoSchedule"}]}}}}'
```

infra-bot: [deployment] inference-deploy (dev) patched at 06:20 UTC

ryan: for the node patch (B) I suggest an ephemeral nodegroup change: add taint `node.kubernetes.io/gpu=present:NoSchedule` back to the new nodes, and also set `accelerator=present` so both keys are present. Example cloud-init snippet included in node bootstrap.

sasha: opened INFRA-4721 to track: normalize taint/label schemas and harden the mutating webhook so it preserves nodeAffinity. Added E2E that fails if a pod with toleration for either key schedules to a non-accelerator node.

marta: after the toleration patch in dev, 3/3 pods scheduled on the GPU node as expected. :white_check_mark:

kai: rolling the toleration change to staging now, will coordinate with autoscaler team to avoid double-scaling while we patch nodegroups.

ryan: long-term: we should standardize on one taint key (prefer `accelerator=present`) and write a migration job that updates existing pod specs or injects tolerations via a reconciler. Also add a release note for scheduler bumps that change predicate ordering.

sasha: agreed. I'll add the migration plan to INFRA-4721 and tag @platform and @autoscaler. Also scheduling regression test added to the canary pipeline.

kai: thanks all. main takeaways: watch for taint/label renames + admission webhooks interfering with node affinity. Quick fix applied, follow-up in INFRA-4721.
